source.title: Interpretable Safety Alignment via SAE-Constructed Low-Rank Subspace Adaptation
source.authors: Dian-Yun Wang; Qing-Sen Ma; Yu-Hu Shang; Zhi-Feng Lu; Lechen Ning; Zhenbo Xu; Hui-Jia Wu; Zhao-Feng He

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The rank ablation reports that rank 1 performs worse than higher ranks and the authors interpret it as recovering only one direction of a multidimensional safety subspace. This refines the single-direction account, although it tests their trained SAE-guided adapter rather than the original residual-stream intervention.
record.gate_note: The paper also cites the original refusal-direction work, but cited results are not recorded as rows. The SAILS main results and most ablations evaluate the paper's own alignment method; the rank ablation is retained because it directly compares rank 1 with higher-rank safety subspaces. Activation steering results are retained as related findings but do not measure refusal rates or establish the dimensionality of the refusal mechanism.
record.test_reason: The paper uses the low-rank safety-structure literature, including Arditi et al., only as motivation for its own SAE-initialised LoRA alignment method (SAILS), and reports that method's performance. The rank sweep (Table 6) varies the LoRA adapter rank, a training-capacity hyperparameter of the authors' own method. It does not ablate or add a difference-in-means refusal direction in the residual stream, and it does not measure how many directions mediate refusal in the model. The SAE steering experiment reports Perspective API toxicity, not refusal rates. Theorem 1 (a mean difference recovers one direction of an r-dimensional subspace) is derived under the paper's assumed generative model, with r≥2 assumed rather than shown for refusal. So no row tests any version, and the record's T5/'tests' guess is not supported.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct but misweighted. The headline conclusion is that SAILS, which initialises LoRA's B matrix from SAE decoder directions, reaches RLHF-level safety (up to 99.6% on Gemma-2-9B) while updating 0.19–0.24% of parameters. The authors also prove that SAE-based subspace identification can have arbitrarily small error, while mean-difference identification has an error floor. The 'rank-1 recovers only one direction' remark is a side interpretation in Appendix B.2.
record.recipe_differences: Uses safe-versus-unsafe SAE feature differences to construct a multi-direction subspace for LoRA initialization and training, rather than finding and projecting out or adding one residual-stream difference-in-means direction. It also reports SAE-feature activation steering.
record.method_sensitivity: Rank changes the rank-ablation results: safety rate peaks at rank 16 and declines at rank 32. Target-layer selection changes results (Table 2), and SAE width changes results (Table 5). Steering strength changes toxicity in the reported intervention.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling the top 50 safety-relevant SAE features at layer 15 of unaligned Gemma-2-2B changes toxicity: γ=2.5 lowers toxicity from 0.42 to 0.28, and suppression raises it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features selected by aligned-minus-unaligned activation differences causally modulate harmful-output toxicity in base models.

fits_no_version.finding: For the authors' SAE-initialised LoRA safety fine-tuning on Gemma-2-2B, safety rate rises from rank 1 (86.2%) to rank 16 (96.8%), then drops at rank 32 (92.4%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety fine-tuning via subspace-initialised LoRA benefits from adapter rank above 1, up to a point.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The rank evidence is from a single model under the paper's own SAILS training setup; uncertainty estimates are not reported. The activation-steering outcomes measure toxicity rather than refusal rates, and the suppression values by scaling factor are not given in text.
record.rows_left_out: Table 1's main SAILS outcomes, Table 2 layer ablation, Table 3 component ablation, and Table 5 SAE-width ablation are not included as rows because they evaluate the proposed alignment method rather than directly test the claim versions. Cited findings from prior work are also excluded.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of a difference-in-means refusal direction, and no refusal rates on harmful or harmless prompts.
No weight-edit or abliteration of released models.
GCG attack success is reported only for the authors' own aligned models; there is no test of whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction.
No measurement of refusal geometry (affine, cone, or multiple directions). The LoRA rank sweep and Theorem 1 do not test this; the theorem assumes a multi-dimensional subspace.
Harmfulness judgment and the refusal decision are not separated.
No transfer of a refusal direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
No comparison of training regimes for refusal-direction existence.

record.verdict_notes: Arditi et al. is cited only as motivation. Theorem 1 formalises the idea that a single mean-difference vector spans one dimension of an assumed r≥2 safety subspace. This is a modelling assumption, not evidence about refusal in real models, so it is not treated as a T5 argument. The judge is kimi-k2, and no uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate or add the original harmful-minus-harmless residual-stream direction across layers and positions, and does not measure refusal of harmless requests.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
Tests LoRA subspace rank in SAILS, not affine/cone geometry or whether a dominant refusal direction is supplemented by particular other directions.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Cross-family evaluation is reported, but no transfer test of the specified refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
Does not compare how or when refusal training determines whether a removable direction exists.
Does not test reasoning models for the single-direction claim.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Train SAILS with the specified LoRA rank; rank-selection ablation.
rows.note: The table also reports harmfulness 1.58 and high-risk rate 13.0%. The authors say rank 1 recovers only one direction of the multidimensional safety subspace.
rows.check: LoRA rank of the authors' own SAILS fine-tuning is a hyperparameter of their method, not a measure of refusal-direction dimensionality. Safety rate after training cannot show whether refusal is mediated by one or several directions. This is an own-method ablation, not a test of V4.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Amplify the top 50 identified safety-related SAE feature activations by scaling them at inference.

conditions.value: subset of HEx-PHI harmful prompts; size not stated

rows.measure: Toxicity score measured by Perspective API
rows.note: This intervention changes a set of SAE features and reports toxicity, not refusal rate or a test of the specified single residual-stream direction.
rows.check: Scales 50 SAE features and measures toxicity on an unaligned base model, not refusal rate along a harmful-minus-harmless direction. The prompt-subset size is not stated.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Suppress the top 50 identified safety-related SAE feature activations by scaling them below their unmodified level at inference.

conditions.value: subset of HEx-PHI harmful prompts; size not stated

rows.measure: Toxicity score measured by Perspective API
rows.value: The text says toxicity increases as γ decreases toward 0; values by scaling factor are not stated.
rows.note: The text describes the trend but does not give the values for γ = 0 or 0.5. This is not a refusal-rate measurement or a test of the specified single residual-stream direction.
rows.check: Values for γ<1 are not given. The row measures toxicity of SAE-feature suppression, not refusal.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: SAILS ranks 4, 8, and 16 compared with rank 1
reader_labels.reason: Safety rate rises from 86.2% at rank 1 to 91.5%, 92.2%, and 96.8% at ranks 4, 8, and 16, respectively (R1–R4), consistent with a higher-rank safety subspace performing better than rank 1 in this setting.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Rank 1 and rank 32 in the Gemma-2-2B rank sweep
reader_labels.reason: Rank 1 still reaches 86.2% safety rate, while rank 32 falls below rank 16 at 92.4%; the results do not show that one direction has no effect or that increasing the number of directions always helps (R1, R5).
